title: 00 — CI/CD & Azure for .NET Developers: Index
html:
00 — CI/CD & Azure for .NET Developers: Index

Audience: a .NET developer who needs to own the path from git push to production on Azure, and be able to explain and defend every step of it. Scope: CI/CD concepts → GitHub Actions → Azure DevOps → the Azure services a .NET developer actually uses daily.

⚠️ Currency note: written from knowledge current to ~mid-2026. Azure service names, SKUs, portal navigation, and default runtime versions change frequently. Anything marked 🔄 is version-sensitive — verify against the current Microsoft Learn docs before relying on it in a design document.

1. The mental model

flowchart LR
    subgraph Dev["Developer loop"]
      C[Code] --> PR[Pull request]
    end
    subgraph CI["Continuous Integration"]
      PR --> B[Build once]
      B --> T[Test + scan]
      T --> A["Artifact:<br/>container image or zip,<br/>immutable tag"]
    end
    subgraph CD["Continuous Delivery"]
      A --> D1[Dev]
      D1 --> D2[Test/UAT]
      D2 --> APP{Approval}
      APP --> D3[Production]
    end
    subgraph Azure["Azure runtime"]
      D3 --> AS[App Service /<br/>Container Apps /<br/>Functions]
      AS --> KV[(Key Vault)]
      AS --> SQL[(Azure SQL)]
      AS --> SB[[Service Bus]]
      AS --> ST[(Storage)]
      AS --> AI[Application Insights]
    end
    ID[Entra ID / Managed Identity] -.authenticates everything.-> Azure
    ID -.OIDC federation.-> CI

Two ideas hold the whole thing together:

  1. Build once, promote the same artifact. The bytes that pass your tests in dev must be the bytes that run in production. Configuration is injected at runtime, never baked in. Rebuilding per environment means production runs something that was never tested.
  2. Identity, not secrets. Modern Azure work replaces connection strings and client secrets with managed identity (for workloads) and workload identity federation / OIDC (for pipelines). If there's no secret, there's nothing to leak or rotate.

2. File map

# File Covers
00 00_INDEX This file
01 01_CICD_FUNDAMENTALS Concepts, pipeline anatomy, branching, versioning, testing gates, deployment strategies, database changes, secrets, metrics
02 02_GITHUB_ACTIONS Workflow syntax, triggers, jobs, matrix, caching, artifacts, reusable workflows, composite actions, environments, OIDC to Azure, security hardening, full .NET + Angular pipelines
03 03_AZURE_DEVOPS YAML pipelines, stages/jobs/steps, templates, variable groups, service connections, environments and approvals, Artifacts feeds, Repos policies, Boards, migration to/from GitHub
04 04_AZURE_FUNDAMENTALS Tenant/subscription/RG hierarchy, regions and AZs, ARM/Bicep, RBAC, tagging, cost management, Well-Architected Framework, networking basics
05 05_ENTRA_ID_AND_IDENTITY Entra ID objects, app registrations, service principals, managed identity, RBAC vs Graph permissions, OAuth flows, protecting an ASP.NET Core API, calling downstream APIs
06 06_APP_SERVICE_AND_HOSTING App Service plans, deployment slots, scaling, configuration, networking, health checks; Container Apps, AKS, and how to choose
07 07_AZURE_FUNCTIONS Isolated worker model, triggers and bindings, hosting plans (Consumption/Premium/Flex/Dedicated), scaling, cold start, Durable Functions, testing, gotchas
08 08_SERVICE_BUS_AND_MESSAGING Service Bus queues/topics, sessions, dedup, DLQ, peek-lock; Event Grid vs Event Hubs vs Storage Queues; patterns
09 09_AZURE_STORAGE Blob/Table/Queue/File, access tiers, SAS types, lifecycle management, performance, Azure.Storage.Blobs SDK usage
10 10_KEY_VAULT_AND_CONFIG Key Vault secrets/keys/certificates, RBAC, soft delete, rotation; App Configuration, feature flags, ASP.NET Core integration
11 11_AZURE_DATA_SERVICES Azure SQL (tiers, DTU vs vCore, elastic pools), Cosmos DB (partitioning, RUs, consistency), Cache for Redis
12 12_OBSERVABILITY_AND_OPERATIONS Application Insights, Log Analytics, KQL you'll actually write, alerts, autoscale, diagnostics, cost control
13 13_CHECKLISTS_AND_INTERVIEW_QA Production-readiness checklists + ~50 CI/CD and Azure interview questions with answers

3. Reading paths

"I need to build a pipeline this week" → 01 → 02 (GitHub) or 03 (Azure DevOps) → 05 (for OIDC auth) → 10 (secrets).

"I need to deploy a .NET API to Azure properly" → 04 → 06 → 05 → 10 → 12.

"I'm being interviewed on Azure" → 13 first (it tells you what you don't know), then the files it points you at.

"I want the whole picture" → in order, 01 → 13.

4. Conventions

Marker Meaning
⚠️ A mistake that is common, plausible, and expensive
🔄 Version-sensitive — verify against current docs
💡 A recommendation with a stated reason
🔍 How this is probed in an interview
🧪 A command to verify it yourself

All CLI examples use az (Azure CLI). Infrastructure examples use Bicep rather than raw ARM JSON, because Bicep is the current Azure-native IaC language and compiles to ARM. Terraform equivalents are noted where the choice matters.

5. The ten things that matter most

If you read nothing else in this set:

  1. Build once, promote the artifact. Config comes from the environment.
  2. Use managed identity everywhere. No connection strings, no client secrets, nothing to rotate.
  3. Use OIDC/workload identity federation for pipeline → Azure authentication. Never a long-lived service principal secret in a CI variable.
  4. Every deployment must be backward compatible for one version (expand → migrate → contract), or you cannot roll back.
  5. Deployment slots with a warm-up are the cheapest zero-downtime deploy on App Service — but understand what a swap does and doesn't carry across.
  6. Key Vault references in App Service configuration let you use secrets without your code knowing Key Vault exists.
  7. Application Insights with a correlation ID is what makes production debuggable. Add it before you need it.
  8. Set an explicit timeout, retry policy, and circuit breaker on every Azure SDK call — the defaults are not what you want.
  9. Tag everything (owner, environment, cost centre) or you will never explain the bill.
  10. A backup you haven't restored is a hypothesis. Schedule the restore drill.
